title: Police powers: s135, s136 and places of safety
blurb: Tell s135 from s136, apply the 24-hour limit and its extension, and protect children from police cells.
question: Police bring Tom, 16, to the health-based place of safety at 21:00 under section 136 after finding him on a motorway bridge. The suite is busy and an officer asks whether Tom could wait in a police station overnight. What is the correct response?

teach.body: Section 136 lets a police officer remove a person who appears to have a mental disorder and to be in immediate need of care or control to a place of safety, from anywhere except where someone lives. Section 135(1) is a warrant, granted by a magistrate on an AMHP's sworn information, to enter private premises and remove a person. In plain English: s136 is for public places, s135 is for behind a front door.

teach.caption: Under s136(1C) the officer must, if practicable, consult a doctor, registered nurse, AMHP or other prescribed person first.

children.label: s136 available
children.sub: Immediate need of care or control

children.label: s136 not available

teach.h: Police stations as places of safety
head: Who
Rule
rows: Not allowed in a police station (s136A(1))
Only if behaviour poses imminent risk of serious injury or death
And no other place of safety can reasonably be expected to manage
Authorised by an officer of at least inspector rank
Healthcare professional present; checks at least every 30 minutes
teach.caption: Places of Safety Regulations 2017. An extension at a police station also needs a superintendent's approval (s136B(3)).

teach.body: Detention at a place of safety is for the person to be examined by a doctor and interviewed by an AMHP, and for arrangements for their care to be made (s136(2)). The outcome may be informal admission, an application under s2 or s3, or discharge with community follow-up. The person can be moved between places of safety within the same period (s136(3)).

Tom is 16, so he cannot be taken to or kept at a police station under any circumstances (s136A). He stays at the health-based place of safety. His 24 hours started at 21:00 when he arrived. If his condition (for example intoxication) makes assessment impracticable, the examining doctor can extend detention by up to 12 hours before the 24 hours end. Staff involve his parents and a CAMHS-experienced doctor and AMHP.

teach.text: The old 72-hour limit for s135 and s136 changed to 24 hours (plus up to 12) on 11 December 2017. The 2015 Code still says 72 hours because it predates the change: the Act wins. And the extension is the DOCTOR's decision, needing a superintendent's approval only when the assessment is at a police station.

items: s136: public places and anywhere except a dwelling; officer consults a health professional first if practicable.
s135(1): magistrate's warrant on an AMHP's information; AMHP and a doctor accompany the officer.
24 hours from arrival, extendable by the examining doctor by up to 12 hours.
Under-18s never go to a police station as a place of safety; adults only in tightly limited cases.

summary: You can now distinguish s135 and s136, apply the 24-hour period and the 12-hour extension, and explain the strict rules on police stations, including the complete bar for under-18s. You know what the period of detention is for and who decides on an extension.

A.q: What is the maximum period a person can be detained at a place of safety under section 136 before any extension?
A.why: Section 136(2A): the permitted period is 24 hours from arrival at the place of safety, extendable under s136B.

whyNot.0: 12 hours is the maximum extension, added to the 24 hours.
whyNot.1: 72 hours was the limit before the Policing and Crime Act 2017 changes in December 2017.
whyNot.2: 6 hours is the nurse's s5(4) holding power.

A.q: Where may a police officer NOT use section 136?
A.why: Section 136(1A): the power cannot be used in any house, flat or room where a person is living, or its private yard, garden, garage or outhouse.

whyNot.0: An emergency department is not a dwelling, so s136 can be used there.
whyNot.1: A railway platform is a public place where s136 applies.
whyNot.3: A car park is not a dwelling, so s136 applies.

A.q: Who lays the information on oath before a magistrate to obtain a section 135(1) warrant?
A.why: Section 135(1): the justice of the peace acts on information on oath laid by an AMHP.

whyNot.0: Police execute the warrant; they do not apply for a s135(1) warrant.
whyNot.2: A doctor accompanies the officer but does not lay the information.
whyNot.3: The nearest relative has no power to apply for a s135(1) warrant.

B.q: Mr Reid arrives at the health-based place of safety at 10:00 under section 136. He is too intoxicated to assess. What is the latest time his detention could lawfully continue to if the doctor authorises the maximum extension?
B.why: 24 hours from arrival (10:00 next day) plus a maximum 12-hour extension authorised by the examining doctor gives 22:00 the next day (s136(2A), s136B).

whyNot.1: That is the end of the 24 hours without an extension.
whyNot.2: A 72-hour period no longer applies to s136.
whyNot.3: That would be a 6-hour extension; the maximum is 12 hours.

B.q: Who can authorise an extension of detention under section 136B?
options: The AMHP who is leading the Mental Health Act assessment
The doctor responsible for the examination
The nurse in charge of the suite
B.why: Section 136B(1): the registered medical practitioner responsible for the examination may authorise up to 12 more hours, if the person's condition makes assessment impracticable in time.

whyNot.0: Police approval (at superintendent rank) is needed only when the assessment is at a police station; it is still the doctor's authorisation.
whyNot.1: The AMHP interviews the person but does not authorise the extension.
whyNot.3: The nurse in charge has no power to extend place-of-safety detention.

B.q: Before using section 136, what must the police officer do if it is practicable?
options: Obtain a warrant from a magistrate
Consult a health professional such as a nurse
Secure written consent from an officer of inspector rank
B.why: Section 136(1C): the constable must, if practicable, consult a registered medical practitioner, registered nurse, AMHP or other prescribed person.

whyNot.0: Section 136 is a power without a warrant.
whyNot.2: There is no duty on the officer to inform the nearest relative first.
whyNot.3: Inspector authorisation relates to using a police station for an adult, not to using s136.

C.q: Tom, 16, is detained under section 136. The health-based place of safety is full and an officer suggests the custody suite until morning. What is the correct position?
options: Allowed if an inspector authorises it
Allowed if a nurse checks him every 30 minutes
Allowed for 12 hours as an extension
Not allowed for a person under 18
C.why: Section 136A(1): a child (under 18) may not be removed to, kept at or taken to a police station as a place of safety.

whyNot.0: Inspector authorisation is one of the adult conditions; it cannot be used for a child.
whyNot.1: 30-minute welfare checks are an adult condition and do not make it lawful for a child.
whyNot.2: The extension rules do not permit a police station for a child.

C.q: An AMHP is concerned that Ms Fox, who lives alone and appears very unwell, is not caring for herself and will not open her door. What is the appropriate legal step?
options: Ask police to use section 136 at her flat
Use section 5(4) at her front door
Wait for her to leave the flat
C.why: Section 135(1)(b) covers a person believed to have a mental disorder who is unable to care for themselves and living alone; the warrant allows entry and removal to a place of safety.

whyNot.0: Section 136 cannot be used in the place where the person lives.
whyNot.3: Delay leaves a person at risk when a lawful route exists.

C.q: An adult is held at a police station as a place of safety because of imminent risk of serious injury. The assessment is to take place there and the doctor wants to extend detention by 12 hours. What extra approval is required?
C.why: Section 136B(3): where the person is at a police station and the assessment is there, the doctor can extend only with approval from an officer of superintendent rank or above.

whyNot.0: No court order is needed for an extension.
whyNot.1: The AMHP's agreement is not the statutory requirement for this extension.
whyNot.3: The nearest relative has no role in authorising an extension.

reteach.title: Door, clock and age
reteach.question: Three checks answer most place-of-safety questions. What are they?

blocks.body: DOOR: is the person in a home? Then s136 cannot be used; an AMHP seeks a s135(1) warrant. CLOCK: 24 hours from arrival, plus up to 12 more if the doctor judges assessment impracticable. AGE: under 18 means no police station, whatever the pressure on beds.

items.label: welfare checks for an adult in a police station

blocks.text: Do not trust the 72-hour figure in the 2015 Code for s135 and s136: the Act was changed in December 2017.

explain.body: A constable may remove a person who appears mentally disordered and in immediate need of care or control to a place of safety, or keep them at one, in any place except a dwelling. Consult a health professional first if practicable.

test.q: Which statement about section 136 is correct?
options: It can be used in a hospital waiting room
It needs an AMHP's information laid on oath first
It allows entry to the person's home
test.why: A hospital waiting room is not a dwelling, so s136 can be used there.

whyNot.1: Information on oath is for a s135(1) warrant.
whyNot.3: The period is 24 hours, extendable by 12.

explain.body: A magistrate may issue a warrant on an AMHP's information where a person believed to have a mental disorder is ill-treated, neglected or not under proper control, or unable to care for themselves and living alone. The officer must be accompanied by an AMHP and a doctor.

test.q: When executing a section 135(1) warrant, who must accompany the police officer?
options: The nearest relative and a GP
A paramedic and a social worker
An AMHP and a registered doctor
test.why: Section 135(4): the constable shall be accompanied by an AMHP and a registered medical practitioner.

whyNot.0: The nearest relative is not required to attend.
whyNot.1: The Act names an AMHP and a doctor, not a paramedic.
whyNot.2: Nurses are not the professionals named in s135(4).

explain.body: 24 hours from arrival (or from the decision to keep the person at a place of safety). The examining doctor may add up to 12 hours if the person's condition makes assessment impracticable in time.

test.q: On what ground can the doctor extend place-of-safety detention?
options: No bed is available on the ward
The AMHP is delayed by other urgent work
The nearest relative cannot be contacted in time
test.why: Section 136B(2): the extension is allowed because the person's condition makes it impracticable to carry out or complete the assessment in time.

whyNot.0: Bed availability is not a ground for extension.
whyNot.1: Professional availability is not a lawful ground.
whyNot.3: Contacting the nearest relative is not a ground for extension.

explain.body: Under-18s: not allowed. Adults: only for imminent risk of serious injury or death that no other place of safety can manage, authorised by an inspector or above, with a healthcare professional available and checks at least every 30 minutes.

test.q: For an adult held in a police station as a place of safety, how often must a healthcare professional check their welfare?
test.why: Places of Safety Regulations 2017: welfare checks by a healthcare professional at least every 30 minutes.

whyNot.0: Hourly is the custody officer's review, not the healthcare check.
whyNot.2: 15 minutes is the seclusion observation record interval, not this rule.
whyNot.3: 2 hours is the seclusion nursing review interval.
